grammar[0].fact: German speech tells the past in the Perfekt: *Ich habe gegessen*. The simple past, *ich aß*, lives mostly in books and the news, and in the south it has nearly died out in speech.

opener.caption: Ein Weg durch den Wald, an einem Sonntag im Mai.
reading.intro: Monday, nine o’clock, at the coffee machine in Max’s office. His colleague Tina has had a perfect weekend, as always. Max has too. Then somebody asks to see the photos.
reading.photos[0].caption: Der Sonntagsspaziergang: ein Bild von Carl Spitzweg, um 1841.
reading.photos[1].caption: Am Sonntag auf dem See: Hier ist man im Winter gelaufen.
reading.en: Tina: Good morning, Max! What did you do at the weekend? · Max: Oh, lots! On Saturday I tidied the flat. Then I read a book. A thick book. · Tina: Great. On Saturday I did yoga and baked bread. On Sunday we had breakfast in the forest. · Max: In the forest? Super. I did a lot on Sunday too. I learned Spanish and called my mother. · Chef: Good morning! Spanish? I like that, Max. Show me your photos from the weekend! · Max: Photos? I … I didn’t take many pictures. · Chef: Here on your phone: that’s your sofa. That’s your sofa too. And that’s a pizza on your sofa. · Max: Yes. I ordered that in Spanish. · Tina: Honestly, Max: I only slept too. I bought the bread. · Chef: And me? I read emails all Sunday. Yours.
reading.fact: At work, Germans say *Schönes Wochenende!* on Friday, and on Monday the honest answer to “how was it?” is *Nichts Besonderes*. Sunday itself is officially quiet: no drilling, no mowing the lawn, and in many places no glass in the bottle bank.

document.caption: Eintrittspreise: Was kostet das Museum am Sonntag?
document.intro: A real price board at a small museum in Austria. *Erwachsene* are adults, *Schüler* are pupils, *gratis* means free. Everyone in Germany and Austria pays something different, so read to the end.
document.fact: Many German museums have a free day, often the first Sunday of the month. Then you can stay for ten minutes without feeling guilty.
